newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia's Russian peacekeepers fear new war.
newsitem.headline: Georgia's Russian peacekeepers fear new war.

text.p: Russian peacekeepers enforcing a fragile peace between Georgia and its breakaway Abkhazia region on the eastern shore of the Black Sea say pulling them out would mean new war.
Though new peace talks under way in Geneva, just a week remains until a deadline for the Russians' withdrawal following an ultimatum from the Georgian government.

Georgia has demanded the 1,500-strong Russian force leave after its present mandate expires on July 31 if it does not agree to step up its activity, including helping ethnic Georgian refugees to return and patrolling a wider area of Abkhazia.

Moscow has so far rejected the demands, citing Abkhaz objections. The Abkhaz say giving the peacekeepers more powers would threaten the de facto independence they won in a bitter 1992-93 conflict with Georgian troops which cost 10,000 lives.
"The Abkhaz say they will defend their territory if we leave. That would mean it's very possible war could resume," the Russian force commander General Dolya Babenkov told Reuters.
"If there is no replacement for the Russians, I can tell you 100 percent there will be war," said one of the hundred or so foreign U.N. observers stationed in Abkhazia.
"These people hate each other. They'd tear each other apart like dogs if we weren't here," said Valery, a 19-year Russian conscript with a Kalashnikov slung over his shoulder.
The first ones to suffer, Russian soldiers say, would be the 50,000 ethnic Georgians in the "security zone" between Abkhazia and Georgia. The Russians patrol the area in armoured vehicles.
"If we weren't here, the Abkhaz would be. And that would mean all these people would run like rabbits," Valery said, as he pointed at an old woman pushing a cart along the road.
Most of the Georgians living in the security zone fled the war, fearing ethnic cleansing, and felt secure enough to return only after the Russian force was deployed in 1994.
Life is far from normal.
Power supplies are sporadic and there is little social life. The eerie quiet in the main town, Gali, is broken only by the creak of lifeless traffic signals swinging in the wind.
Most residents do not dare venture out after mid-afternoon, fearing violence. Many homes are burnt-out shells, looted and torched by the advancing Abkhaz at the war's end.

But it beats the lot of tens of thousands of Georgians stuck in cramped refugee accomodation elsewhere. They used to make up 45 percent of Abkhazia's population but most fled the separatist takeover. Only those with homes in the security zone returned.
"If they leave there will be horrors here," said 78-year old Eteri, wearily pushing her cart under a light drizzle.

The Georgian-Abkhaz dispute simmered for years under Soviet rule. Georgian forces swept into the subtropical Black Sea region in 1992 to put down demands for more autonomy but were finally driven out by the Abkhaz, who had Russian military help.
Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze completed a trip this week to the United States, where he sought support for an international force to replace or complement the Russians.
But Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba flatly rejected the idea and vowed his army would repel any incursion.

Shevardnadze said many Western leaders had urged him to let the Russians stay on, warning renewed violence could upset Georgia's tentative return to economic growth and plans for the building of a lucrative oil pipeline across Georgian territory.
But the former Soviet foreign minister still must deal with a Georgian parliament where many see the Russian force as simply reinforcing the divide with Abkhazia.
U.N Secretary General Kofi Annan urged both sides to seek compromise on Wednesday. But previous talks have stalled over Abkhaz desires for more autonomy than Georgia will tolerate.
